claim: Most adult Langerhans cells (LCs) in zebrafish originated from the ventral wall of the dorsal aorta (VDA).
source: Here, using a laser-mediated temporal-spatial resolved cell labeling method, we demonstrated that most adult LCs originated from the ventral wall of the dorsal aorta (VDA), an equivalent to the mouse aorta, gonads, and mesonephros (AGM), where both hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and non-HSC progenitors are generated.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from IR-LEGO-CreER-loxP fate mapping experiments showing ~80% of adult LCs were GFP+ after VDA labeling.

claim: The VDA in zebrafish is equivalent to the mouse aorta, gonads, and mesonephros (AGM).
source: Here, using a laser-mediated temporal-spatial resolved cell labeling method, we demonstrated that most adult LCs originated from the ventral wall of the dorsal aorta (VDA), an equivalent to the mouse aorta, gonads, and mesonephros (AGM), where both hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and non-HSC progenitors are generated.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about the homology between zebrafish VDA and mammalian AGM.

claim: Both hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and non-HSC progenitors are generated in the VDA.
source: Here, using a laser-mediated temporal-spatial resolved cell labeling method, we demonstrated that most adult LCs originated from the ventral wall of the dorsal aorta (VDA), an equivalent to the mouse aorta, gonads, and mesonephros (AGM), where both hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and non-HSC progenitors are generated.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about hematopoiesis in the VDA/AGM region.

claim: The appearance of LCs in adult zebrafish was correlated with the development of HSCs.
source: Further fine-fate mapping analysis revealed that the appearance of LCs in adult zebrafish was correlated with the development of HSCs, but not T cell progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from single-spot VDA labeling and temporal analysis showing LCs appear in HSC-labeled groups.

claim: The appearance of LCs in adult zebrafish was not correlated with T cell progenitors.
source: Further fine-fate mapping analysis revealed that the appearance of LCs in adult zebrafish was correlated with the development of HSCs, but not T cell progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that Group I-B fish (labeled with non-HSC T cell progenitors) did not contain significant GFP+ LCs.

claim: The appearance of tissue-resident macrophages in the brain, liver, heart, and gut of adult zebrafish was correlated with HSCs.
source: Finally, we showed that the appearance of tissue-resident macrophages in the brain, liver, heart, and gut of adult zebrafish was also correlated with HSCs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from fate mapping and transplantation experiments showing tissue-resident macrophages in these organs are found predominantly in HSC-labeled groups.

claim: The results of this study challenged the EMP-origin theory for LCs.
source: Thus, the results of our study challenged the EMP-origin theory for LCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing HSC correlation and limited PBI (EMP source) contribution to adult LCs.

claim: Langerhans cells are resident macrophages in skin epidermis with immune-stimulatory capacities.
source: Langerhans cells (LCs) are resident macrophages in skin epidermis, where they have immune-stimulatory capacities.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about LC function.

claim: Upon activation, LCs migrate from the epidermis to the skin-draining lymph nodes to present antigens to T cells under both steady and inflammatory conditions.
source: Under both steady and inflammatory conditions, upon activation, LCs migrate from the epidermis to the skin-draining lymph nodes to present antigens to T cells, resulting in the activation of acquired immunity (Hemmi et al., 2001; Merad et al., 2008; Romani et al., 2010; Stoitzner et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LC migration to lymph nodes results in the activation of acquired immunity.
source: Under both steady and inflammatory conditions, upon activation, LCs migrate from the epidermis to the skin-draining lymph nodes to present antigens to T cells, resulting in the activation of acquired immunity (Hemmi et al., 2001; Merad et al., 2008; Romani et al., 2010; Stoitzner et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Several studies have suggested that LCs confer immune tolerance of the skin.
source: In addition, several studies have suggested that LCs also confer immune tolerance of the skin (Bobr et al., 2010; Chopin and Nutt, 2015; Kaplan et al., 2005; Merad et al., 2008; Romani et al., 2012; Shklovskaya et al., 2011; van der Aar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LCs dampen the immune response under steady-state conditions but activate the response upon challenge.
source: The biological significance of the opposing roles of LCs remains unclear, but it is thought that LCs dampen the immune response under steady-state conditions, but activate the response upon challenge (Seneschal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents a hypothesis in the field.

claim: LCs were identified over 100 years ago.
source: Although LCs were identified over 100 years ago, their origins have been debated ever since their discovery.
evidence: This is established historical knowledge about LC discovery.

claim: The origins of LCs have been debated since their discovery.
source: Although LCs were identified over 100 years ago, their origins have been debated ever since their discovery.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ongoing scientific debate.

claim: LCs were initially considered to be nerve cells in the skin.
source: Initially, LCs were considered to be nerve cells in the skin (Langerhans, 1868) and subsequently were thought to have a melanocyte or keratinocyte origin (Birbeck et al., 1961; Reams and Tompkins, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citation to historical work.

claim: LCs were subsequently thought to have a melanocyte or keratinocyte origin.
source: Initially, LCs were considered to be nerve cells in the skin (Langerhans, 1868) and subsequently were thought to have a melanocyte or keratinocyte origin (Birbeck et al., 1961; Reams and Tompkins, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical studies.

claim: The hematopoietic origin of LCs was revealed in 1979.
source: The hematopoietic origin of LCs was not revealed until 1979, when researchers observed that donor-derived LCs were present in the skin of lethally-irradiated mice transplanted with allogeneic or semi-allogeneic hematopoietic precursors (Frelinger et al., 1979; Katz et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original studies.

claim: Donor-derived LCs were present in the skin of lethally-irradiated mice transplanted with allogeneic or semi-allogeneic hematopoietic precursors.
source: The hematopoietic origin of LCs was not revealed until 1979, when researchers observed that donor-derived LCs were present in the skin of lethally-irradiated mice transplanted with allogeneic or semi-allogeneic hematopoietic precursors (Frelinger et al., 1979; Katz et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The observation of donor-derived LCs in transplanted mice led to the hypothesis that LCs were replenished continually by circulating monocytes.
source: This led to the hypothesis that LCs were replenished continually by circulating monocytes (Romani et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference from the transplantation data, supported by citation.

claim: Most LCs in lethally-irradiated mice reconstituted with congenic hematopoietic precursors were of host origin.
source: The first clue came from transplantation studies by Merad et al., who reported that most LCs in lethally-irradiated mice reconstituted with either congenic hematopoietic precursors or T cell-free allogenic precursors were of a host origin (Merad et al., 2004; Merad et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Merad et al. studies.

claim: Most LCs in lethally-irradiated mice reconstituted with T cell-free allogenic precursors were of host origin.
source: The first clue came from transplantation studies by Merad et al., who reported that most LCs in lethally-irradiated mice reconstituted with either congenic hematopoietic precursors or T cell-free allogenic precursors were of a host origin (Merad et al., 2004; Merad et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Merad et al. studies.

claim: LCs turn over slowly in steady-state.
source: Subsequent studies further documented that LCs turn over slowly in steady-state.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the following sentence.

claim: LCs are replenished by a small number of proliferative LC precursors residing in the skin.
source: In fact, LCs are replenished by a small number of proliferative LC precursors residing in the skin, although circulating precursors do contribute to LCs when a severe injury occurs (Chorro et al., 2009; Collin et al., 2006; Ghigo et al., 2013; Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015; Hoeffel et al., 2015; Hoeffel et al., 2012; Kanitakis et al., 2004; Krueger et al., 1983; Schulz et al., 2012; Vishwanath et al., 2006; Yona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Circulating precursors contribute to LCs when a severe injury occurs.
source: In fact, LCs are replenished by a small number of proliferative LC precursors residing in the skin, although circulating precursors do contribute to LCs when a severe injury occurs (Chorro et al., 2009; Collin et al., 2006; Ghigo et al., 2013; Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015; Hoeffel et al., 2015; Hoeffel et al., 2012; Kanitakis et al., 2004; Krueger et al., 1983; Schulz et al., 2012; Vishwanath et al., 2006; Yona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The origin and nature of the proliferative LC precursors remain largely undefined.
source: Despite these studies, the origin and nature of the proliferative LC precursors remain largely undefined.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The self-renewal ability of adult LCs led to the hypothesis that LCs are generated from sources independent of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs).
source: The self-renewal ability of adult LCs led to the hypothesis that LCs are generated from sources independent of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), which are born in the aorta, gonads, and mesonephros (AGM) in mammals (Orkin and Zon, 2008).
evidence: This is an inference from the self-renewal observation, supported by citation.

claim: HSCs are born in the aorta, gonads, and mesonephros (AGM) in mammals.
source: The self-renewal ability of adult LCs led to the hypothesis that LCs are generated from sources independent of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), which are born in the aorta, gonads, and mesonephros (AGM) in mammals (Orkin and Zon, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Hoeffel et al. showed that adult LCs in mice had dual origins: YS primitive monocytes and fetal liver monocytes using Runx1-MER-Cre-MER/Rosa26-YFP reporter mice.
source: This was supported by a recent fate-mapping study by Hoeffel et al., who utilized Runx1-MER-Cre-MER/Rosa26-YFP reporter mice and showed that adult LCs in mice had dual origins: YS primitive monocytes and fetal liver monocytes (Hoeffel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hoeffel et al. study.

claim: Adult LCs in mice were predominantly generated from YS-derived erythro-myeloid precursors (EMPs) according to fate-mapping studies with MER-Cre-MER/Rosa26 reporter systems.
source: Further fate-mapping studies with similar MER-Cre-MER/Rosa26 reporter systems suggested that adult LCs in mice were predominantly generated from YS-derived erythro-myeloid precursors (EMPs) (Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015; Hoeffel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous fate-mapping studies.

claim: The EMP-origin theory was challenged by Sheng et al., who found that most resident macrophages, including LCs, in adult mice were predominantly derived from HSCs using the c-Kit-MER-Cre-MER/Rosa26-YFP reporter system.
source: Yet, this EMP-origin theory was challenged by a recent study by Sheng et al., who utilized the c-Kit-MER-Cre-MER/Rosa26-YFP reporter system to trace the origin of tissue-resident macrophages and found that most resident macrophages, including LCs, in adult mice were predominantly derived from HSCs but not from EMPs (Sheng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sheng et al. study.

claim: Fate-mapping studies using promoter-controlled CreER-loxP tracking systems cannot provide a definitive answer about the origin of LCs because the exact transcription activity of these promoters in the tissue of interest remains to be further elucidated.
source: However, despite their elegant designs, these fate-mapping studies, relied on promoter-controlled CreER-loxP tracking systems. The exact transcription activity of these promoters in the tissue of interest remains to be further elucidated, so such studies cannot provide a definitive answer about the origin of LCs.
evidence: This is a critical assessment and inference about the limitations of previous methods.

claim: Conventional lineage-tracing systems cannot selectively label and distinguish cells from different anatomic locations.
source: Furthermore, conventional lineage-tracing systems cannot selectively label and distinguish cells from different anatomic locations.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of conventional methods based on knowledge of the techniques.

claim: A new cell labeling strategy that can provide both temporal and spatial resolution is required to identify the origin of LCs.
source: These shortcomings have hindered the identification of the origin of LCs, so a new cell labeling strategy that can provide both temporal and spatial resolution is required.
evidence: This is an inference from the limitations of existing methods.

claim: Zebrafish experience multiple waves of hematopoiesis similar to mammals.
source: Similar to mammals, zebrafish experience multiple waves of hematopoiesis (Jagannathan-Bogdan and Zon, 2013; Jing and Zon, 2011; Stachura and Traver, 2011; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The first or embryonic hematopoiesis in zebrafish initiates at ~11 hr post fertilization (hpf) in the posterior lateral mesoderm (PLM) and rostral blood island (RBI).
source: The first or embryonic hematopoiesis in the zebrafish initiates at ~11 hr post fertilization (hpf) in the posterior lateral mesoderm (PLM) and rostral blood island (RBI), which are, similar to the mammalian yolk sac (YS), producing embryonic erythroid and myeloid cells respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrafish hematopoiesis.

claim: The PLM and RBI in zebrafish are similar to the mammalian yolk sac (YS), producing embryonic erythroid and myeloid cells respectively.
source: The first or embryonic hematopoiesis in the zebrafish initiates at ~11 hr post fertilization (hpf) in the posterior lateral mesoderm (PLM) and rostral blood island (RBI), which are, similar to the mammalian yolk sac (YS), producing embryonic erythroid and myeloid cells respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the homology between zebrafish and mammalian hematopoietic sites.

claim: The second or definitive wave of hematopoiesis in zebrafish occurs at ~28 hpf in the ventral wall of the dorsal aorta (VDA).
source: The second or definitive wave of hematopoiesis occurs at ~28 hpf in the ventral wall of the dorsal aorta (VDA), a tissue equivalent to the mammalian AGM (Orkin and Zon, 2008), and gives rise to HSCs capable of generating all blood cell types during fetal life and adulthood.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrafish hematopoiesis supported by citation.

claim: The VDA gives rise to HSCs capable of generating all blood cell types during fetal life and adulthood.
source: The second or definitive wave of hematopoiesis occurs at ~28 hpf in the ventral wall of the dorsal aorta (VDA), a tissue equivalent to the mammalian AGM (Orkin and Zon, 2008), and gives rise to HSCs capable of generating all blood cell types during fetal life and adulthood.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HSC function.

claim: A third or intermediate wave of hematopoiesis in zebrafish generates EMPs and initiates autonomously from the posterior blood island (PBI) at around 30 hpf.
source: A third or intermediate wave of hematopoiesis, which generates EMPs, is believed to initiate autonomously from the posterior blood island (PBI) at around 30 hpf and produces erythroid and myeloid cells during both embryonic and fetal development (Bertrand et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The intermediate wave of hematopoiesis produces erythroid and myeloid cells during both embryonic and fetal development.
source: A third or intermediate wave of hematopoiesis, which generates EMPs, is believed to initiate autonomously from the posterior blood island (PBI) at around 30 hpf and produces erythroid and myeloid cells during both embryonic and fetal development (Bertrand et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Zebrafish's conserved hematopoietic program, genetic amenability, and imaging feasibility make it an excellent model system for fate-mapping studies of LCs.
source: Thus, its conserved hematopoietic program, genetic amenability, and imaging feasibility have made zebrafish an excellent model system to use for fate-mapping studies of LCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of the zebrafish model.

claim: The RBI was the primary source for LCs at early embryonic stages (4 dpf).
source: Tracing results showed that, although the RBI was the primary source for LCs at early embryonic stages, most (~80% LCs are GFP+) LCs in the adult zebrafish (≥3 months old) were of a VDA origin and only limited numbers of adult LCs were derived from the RBI and PBI, compared with non-heat-shocked control fish (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Approximately 80% of LCs in adult zebrafish (≥3 months old) were of VDA origin.
source: Tracing results showed that, although the RBI was the primary source for LCs at early embryonic stages, most (~80% LCs are GFP+) LCs in the adult zebrafish (≥3 months old) were of a VDA origin and only limited numbers of adult LCs were derived from the RBI and PBI, compared with non-heat-shocked control fish (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Only limited numbers of adult LCs were derived from the RBI and PBI.
source: Tracing results showed that, although the RBI was the primary source for LCs at early embryonic stages, most (~80% LCs are GFP+) LCs in the adult zebrafish (≥3 months old) were of a VDA origin and only limited numbers of adult LCs were derived from the RBI and PBI, compared with non-heat-shocked control fish (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: The labeling efficiency of VDA-derived HSPCs was approximately 80%.
source: According to the tracing result that ~80% of adult LCs were labeled, we hypothesized that our labeling efficiency was also about 80%.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The remaining ~20% non-GFP+ LCs were likely derived from unlabeled HSPCs in VDA due to incomplete heat-shock or loxP recombination.
source: The remaining ~20% non-GFP +LCs were likely derived from unlabeled HSPCs in VDA due to the incomplete heat-shock or loxP recombination.
evidence: This is a speculative inference to explain the incomplete labeling.

claim: The percentage of RBI-derived LCs gradually decreased from 4 dpf to 12 dpf.
source: The results showed that the percentage of RBI-derived LCs gradually decreased and only ~7% of LCs were derived from a RBI origin at 12 dpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: Only ~7% of LCs were derived from RBI origin at 12 dpf.
source: The results showed that the percentage of RBI-derived LCs gradually decreased and only ~7% of LCs were derived from a RBI origin at 12 dpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: VDA-derived LCs became obvious at 6 dpf.
source: By contrast, the VDA-derived LCs became obvious at 6 dpf and their percentage reached 54% by 12 dpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: The percentage of VDA-derived LCs reached 54% by 12 dpf.
source: By contrast, the VDA-derived LCs became obvious at 6 dpf and their percentage reached 54% by 12 dpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: A small portion of PBI-derived LCs was observed from 6 dpf.
source: A small portion of PBI-derived LCs was observed from 6 dpf.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation.

claim: PBI-derived LCs maintained their percentage at ~15% from 8 dpf to 12 dpf, suggesting limited cell proliferation or input from the PBI.
source: In contrast to the prosperous LCs from the VDA, the PBI-derived LCs maintain their percentage at ~15% from 8 dpf to 12 dpf suggesting limited cell proliferation or input from the PBI (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and inference about the mechanism.

claim: LCs gradually shifted from a RBI origin to a VDA origin during the early larval stages of zebrafish development.
source: Taken together, these data suggested that LCs gradually shifted from a RBI origin to a VDA origin during the early larval stages of zebrafish development.
evidence: This is an inference from the temporal analysis data.

claim: Most DsRedx+ macrophages on the superficial part of adult skin located within the krtt1c19e+ epidermal layer.
source: We found that most DsRedx+ macrophages on the superficial part of the adult skin located within the krtt1c19e+ epidermal layer, suggesting that they were indeed LCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: VDA-derived LCs require Runx1 function.
source: Genetic studies showed that VDA-derived LCs required runx1 and cMyb functions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from runx1 mutant analysis.

claim: VDA-derived LCs require cMyb function.
source: Genetic studies showed that VDA-derived LCs required runx1 and cMyb functions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cmyb mutant analysis.

claim: HSPC formation in the VDA region was severely impaired in runx1W84X mutants.
source: To test this hypothesis, we crossed Tg(hsp70:mCherry-T2a-CreERT2;mpeg1:loxP-DsRedx-loxP-GFP) with runx1W84X mutants, in which HSPC formation in the VDA region was severely impaired (Bertrand et al., 2010; Boisset et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2009; Jin et al., 2009; Kissa and Herbomel, 2010; Sood et al., 2010), and examined the VDA-derived LCs at ~12 dpf.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: There was a reduction of >85% in the density of GFP+ LCs in runx1W84X mutants compared to siblings (7.0 cells/mm2 in mutants versus 53.8 cells/mm2 in siblings).
source: Our results showed a reduction of >85% (7.0 cells/mm2 in the mutants versus 53.8 cells/mm2 in siblings) in the density of GFP+ LCs in runx1W84X mutants (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The total density of LCs in runx1W84X mutants was reduced (57.7 cells/mm2 in mutants versus 173.2 cells/mm2 in siblings).
source: The total density of LCs in runx1W84X mutants was also reduced (57.7 cells/mm2 in the mutants versus 173.2 cells/mm2 in siblings) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: RBI-derived GFP+ LCs showed no obvious differences between runx1W84X mutants and siblings.
source: By contrast, the RBI-derived GFP+ LCs showed no obvious differences between mutants and siblings when heat-shock labeling was performed in the RBI region (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RBI-derived macrophages are not reduced in runx1W84X mutants.
source: This result was not surprising given that the RBI-derived macrophages are not reduced in runx1W84X mutants (Jin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: cmybhkz3 mutants have a developmental delay and cannot survive beyond 1 month of age.
source: Given that cmybhkz3 mutants have a developmental delay and cannot survive beyond 1 month of age (Xu et al., 2015), we assessed the LCs in 20 dpf cmybhkz3 mutants, comparing them with size-matched 12–15 dpf siblings (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: There was a partial reduction in the density of GFP+ LCs in cmybhkz3 mutants (15.2 cells/mm2 in mutants versus 40.4 cells/mm2 in siblings).
source: Our results showed a partial reduction (15.2 cells/mm2 in the mutants versus 40.4 cells/mm2 in siblings) in the density of GFP+ LCs in cmybhkz3 mutants (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The remaining GFP+ LCs in cmybhkz3 mutants might reflect either a cMyb-independent non-stem cell-derived population in VDA or differentiated progenies from residual surviving HSCs.
source: The remaining GFP+ LCs in the mutants might reflect either a cMyb-independent non-stem cell-derived population in VDA or differentiated progenies from the residual surviving HSCs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The total density of LCs in cmybhkz3 mutants was reduced (66.3 cells/mm2 in mutants versus 133.3 cells/mm2 in siblings).
source: The total density of LCs in cmybhkz3 mutants was also reduced (66.3 cells/mm2 in the mutants versus 133.3 cells/mm2 in siblings) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: There was no obvious difference in RBI-derived GFP+ LCs between cmybhkz3 mutants and siblings.
source: Unsurprisingly, there was no obvious difference in RBI-derived GFP+ LCs between the mutants and siblings when heat-shock labeling was performed in the RBI region (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: cMyb is not required for the development of RBI-derived macrophages.
source: This result was consistent with a previous report that cMyb was not required for the development of RBI-derived macrophages (Jin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: cMyb is partially required for VDA-derived LCs.
source: Nevertheless, this result clearly showed that, although it was not absolutely necessary, cMyb was partially required for these cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing partial reduction in cmyb mutants.

claim: Adult LCs in zebrafish likely arose from HSPCs.
source: These data, together with the fate-mapping results, indicated that adult LCs in the zebrafish likely arose from HSPCs.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic and fate-mapping data.

claim: The VDA region contains non-HSC derived T cell progenitors.
source: We previously showed that the VDA region contained non-HSC derived T cell progenitors (Tian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Eight out of 13 fish with single-spot VDA labeling contained abundant GFP+ LCs and were designated the 'HSC Group'.
source: We found that 8 out of the 13 fish contained abundant GFP+ LCs (Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—source data 1). Notably, abundant GFP+ cells were also present in the circulation of these fish suggesting the successful labeling of HSCs (Figure 3D and E, Figure 3—source data 1). This group of fish was designated the 'HSC Group' (Figure 3B–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-E.

claim: Five out of 13 fish with single-spot VDA labeling failed to contain abundant GFP+ LCs and were designated the 'non-HSC Group'.
source: In the remaining five VDA-labeled fish, GFP+ LCs failed to be abundantly detected (Figure 3B and C) and few GFP+ cells were found in the circulation, suggesting a failure of HSC labeling (Figure 3D and E). These fish were defined as the 'non-HSC Group' (Figure 3B–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-E.

claim: The primary population of GFP+ LCs observed in VDA-labeled fish was associated with HSCs.
source: These data indicated that the primary population of GFP+ LCs observed in the VDA-labeled fish was associated with HSCs.
evidence: This is an inference from the single-spot labeling data.

claim: The density of HSCs gradually decreased from the anterior to the posterior VDA.
source: We previously showed that the density of HSCs gradually decreased from the anterior to the posterior VDA (Tian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: 70% of fish labeled at position 1 (P1) of the VDA contained abundant LCs.
source: Our results showed that 70%, 71%, and 54% of the labeled fish contained abundant LCs for the P1, P2, and P3 groups, respectively. By contrast, only 22% of the labeled fish contained abundant LCs in the P4 group (Figure 3G, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: 71% of fish labeled at position 2 (P2) of the VDA contained abundant LCs.
source: Our results showed that 70%, 71%, and 54% of the labeled fish contained abundant LCs for the P1, P2, and P3 groups, respectively. By contrast, only 22% of the labeled fish contained abundant LCs in the P4 group (Figure 3G, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: 54% of fish labeled at position 3 (P3) of the VDA contained abundant LCs.
source: Our results showed that 70%, 71%, and 54% of the labeled fish contained abundant LCs for the P1, P2, and P3 groups, respectively. By contrast, only 22% of the labeled fish contained abundant LCs in the P4 group (Figure 3G, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Only 22% of fish labeled at position 4 (P4) of the VDA contained abundant LCs.
source: Our results showed that 70%, 71%, and 54% of the labeled fish contained abundant LCs for the P1, P2, and P3 groups, respectively. By contrast, only 22% of the labeled fish contained abundant LCs in the P4 group (Figure 3G, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The generation of adult LCs was correlated with the density gradient of HSCs along the VDA.
source: This suggested that the generation of adult LCs was correlated with the density gradient of HSCs along the VDA.
evidence: This is an inference from the position-dependent labeling data.

claim: Non-HSC-derived T cells generate the first wave of T cells.
source: Non-HSC-derived T cells were reported to generate the first wave of T cells, whereas HSCs generate the second wave of T cells after 5 dpf (Tian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: HSCs generate the second wave of T cells after 5 dpf.
source: Non-HSC-derived T cells were reported to generate the first wave of T cells, whereas HSCs generate the second wave of T cells after 5 dpf (Tian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Only in Group I-A and Group II-A were significant GFP+ cells found in the skin.
source: Interestingly, only in Group I-A and Group II-A, but not in Group I-B and Group II-B, were significant GFP+ cells found in the skin (Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: A significant portion of GFP+ cells in the skin showed a ramified LC-like morphology.
source: Although we do not have LC antibodies to specifically distinguish LCs from other GFP+ leukocytes, a significant portion of GFP+ cells showed a ramified LC-like morphology (Figure 4F), suggesting that LCs were labeled in Group I-A and Group II-A.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: 18-19% of leukocytes were GFP+ in Group I-A and Group II-A.
source: We found 18–19% GFP+ leukocytes in Group I-A and Group II-A compared with almost no GFP+ leukocytes in Group I-B and Group II-B and the non-heat-shocked control groups (Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Almost no GFP+ leukocytes were found in Group I-B, Group II-B, and non-heat-shocked control groups.
source: We found 18–19% GFP+ leukocytes in Group I-A and Group II-A compared with almost no GFP+ leukocytes in Group I-B and Group II-B and the non-heat-shocked control groups (Figure 4E and F, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: Adult LCs are associated with HSCs but not non-HSC T cell progenitors.
source: Taken together, our results suggested that adult LCs associated with HSCs but not non-HSC T cell progenitors.
evidence: This is an inference from the temporal labeling experiment with coro1a reporter.

claim: The primary adult tissue-resident macrophages in liver, gut, and heart were derived from VDA, but not from RBI or PBI.
source: Similar to LCs and previously reported microglia (Xu et al., 2015), the primary adult tissue-resident macrophages in liver, gut, and heart were also derived from VDA, but not from RBI or PBI (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: GFP+ macrophages in the liver, gut, heart and brain were primarily found in the HSC group but not the non-HSC group.
source: The results showed that GFP+ macrophages in the liver, gut, heart and even brain were primarily found in the HSC group but not the non-HSC group (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1), suggesting that tissue-resident macrophages in zebrafish spatially correlated with HSCs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Tissue-resident macrophages in zebrafish spatially correlated with HSCs.
source: The results showed that GFP+ macrophages in the liver, gut, heart and even brain were primarily found in the HSC group but not the non-HSC group (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1), suggesting that tissue-resident macrophages in zebrafish spatially correlated with HSCs.
evidence: This is an inference from the single-spot labeling data.

claim: Only fish labeled with HSCs (Group I-A and Group II-A) contained significant numbers of GFP+ cells in brain, liver, heart, and gut.
source: Similar to the results of LCs, only fish labeled with HSCs (Group I-A and Group II-A) contained significant number of GFP+ cells in brain, liver, heart, and gut (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1), suggesting that adult resident macrophages in brain, liver, heart, and gut were associated with HSCs in zebrafish.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Adult resident macrophages in brain, liver, heart, and gut were associated with HSCs in zebrafish.
source: Similar to the results of LCs, only fish labeled with HSCs (Group I-A and Group II-A) contained significant number of GFP+ cells in brain, liver, heart, and gut (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1), suggesting that adult resident macrophages in brain, liver, heart, and gut were associated with HSCs in zebrafish.
evidence: This is an inference from the temporal labeling data with coro1a reporter.

claim: Most GFP+ cells in brain, liver, and heart were Lcp1+.
source: Interestingly, most GFP+ cells were Lcp1+, with the exception of gut GFP+ cells, which only partially overlapped with Lcp1 signals, suggesting that Lcp1 and coro1a marked different sub-populations of leukocytes in the gut.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing colocalization.

claim: Gut GFP+ cells only partially overlapped with Lcp1 signals.
source: Interestingly, most GFP+ cells were Lcp1+, with the exception of gut GFP+ cells, which only partially overlapped with Lcp1 signals, suggesting that Lcp1 and coro1a marked different sub-populations of leukocytes in the gut.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing partial colocalization.

claim: Lcp1 and coro1a mark different sub-populations of leukocytes in the gut.
source: Interestingly, most GFP+ cells were Lcp1+, with the exception of gut GFP+ cells, which only partially overlapped with Lcp1 signals, suggesting that Lcp1 and coro1a marked different sub-populations of leukocytes in the gut.
evidence: This is an inference from the partial overlap observation.

claim: Among 31 surviving transplant recipients, seven did not contain detectable donor-derived DsRedx+ cells.
source: Among the 31 surviving recipients, seven did not contain detectable donor-derived DsRedx+ cells (data not shown), suggesting a failure of long-term reconstitution of donor cells in these recipients.
evidence: This is experimental observation from the transplantation experiment.

claim: The survival of the seven recipients without donor cells was likely due to the recovery of their own hematopoiesis.
source: The survival of these seven recipients was likely due to the recovery of their own hematopoiesis, as shown previously (Sood et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Group I recipients (eight fish) contained abundant donor-derived DsRedx+ cells in their circulation.
source: Group I recipients (eight fish) were those containing abundant donor-derived DsRedx+ cells in their circulation.
evidence: This is the definition of Group I based on experimental observation.

claim: In Group I recipients, a large number of DsRedx+ donor cells were present in the brain (93%), skin (87%), liver (94%), gut (75%), heart (92%), and circulation (84%).
source: In this group, a large number of DsRedx+ donor cells were present in the brain (microglia, 93%), skin (LCs, 87%), liver (94%), gut (75%), heart (92%), and circulation (84%) (Figure 6B and C, Figure 6—source data 1), showing that these Group I recipients were well reconstituted by donor-derived hematopoietic cells, including HSCs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Group I recipients were well reconstituted by donor-derived hematopoietic cells, including HSCs.
source: In this group, a large number of DsRedx+ donor cells were present in the brain (microglia, 93%), skin (LCs, 87%), liver (94%), gut (75%), heart (92%), and circulation (84%) (Figure 6B and C, Figure 6—source data 1), showing that these Group I recipients were well reconstituted by donor-derived hematopoietic cells, including HSCs.
evidence: This is an inference from the high donor cell contribution in multiple tissues.

claim: Group II recipients (16 fish) contained very few DsRedx+ donor cells (~2%) in their circulation.
source: By contrast, Group II recipients (16 fish) contained very few DsRedx+ donor cells (~2%) in their circulation (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 1), indicating that these recipients were reconstituted by donor-derived progenitor cells but not HSCs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Group II recipients were reconstituted by donor-derived progenitor cells but not HSCs.
source: By contrast, Group II recipients (16 fish) contained very few DsRedx+ donor cells (~2%) in their circulation (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 1), indicating that these recipients were reconstituted by donor-derived progenitor cells but not HSCs.
evidence: This is an inference from the low donor cell contribution in circulation.

claim: Group II recipients contained only small numbers of donor-derived DsRedx+ LCs in the skin (7%), liver (16%), gut (5%), and heart (12%).
source: This group of recipients contained only small numbers of donor-derived DsRedx+ LCs in the skin (7%), liver (16%), gut (5%), and heart (12%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the transplantation experiment.

claim: Group II recipients contained ~50% of donor-derived DsRedx+ microglia in the brain.
source: One exception was the brain, which contained ~50% of donor-derived DsRedx+ microglia (Figure 6B and D, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and D.

claim: Adult microglia likely arise from VDA-born HSCs based on spatial restricted cell tracing analysis.
source: However, based on our previous spatial restricted cell tracing analysis, adult microglia also likely arise from the VDA-born HSCs and the HSC-independency we observed in the transplantation assay is likely due to the self-maintenance of microglia (Ajami et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2018), thus myeloid progenitors from donor kidney marrows are sufficient to generate long lasting microglia.
evidence: This is an inference from previous spatial tracing data.

claim: The HSC-independency of microglia observed in the transplantation assay is likely due to the self-maintenance of microglia.
source: However, based on our previous spatial restricted cell tracing analysis, adult microglia also likely arise from the VDA-born HSCs and the HSC-independency we observed in the transplantation assay is likely due to the self-maintenance of microglia (Ajami et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2018), thus myeloid progenitors from donor kidney marrows are sufficient to generate long lasting microglia.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations about microglia self-maintenance.

claim: Myeloid progenitors from donor kidney marrows are sufficient to generate long lasting microglia.
source: However, based on our previous spatial restricted cell tracing analysis, adult microglia also likely arise from the VDA-born HSCs and the HSC-independency we observed in the transplantation assay is likely due to the self-maintenance of microglia (Ajami et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2018), thus myeloid progenitors from donor kidney marrows are sufficient to generate long lasting microglia.
evidence: This is an inference from the transplantation data and knowledge about microglia self-maintenance.

claim: Adult tissue-resident macrophages are largely associated with HSCs during transplantation.
source: Taken together, our data suggested that adult tissue-resident macrophages are largely associated with HSCs during transplantation.
evidence: This is an inference from the transplantation data.

claim: A large portion of adult LCs and other tissue-resident macrophages in zebrafish were derived from an HSC origin.
source: Although we cannot completely rule out the possibility that LCs and other tissue-resident macrophages were derived from non-HSC progenitors, which must be linked with HSCs so closely that they cannot be distinguished by our spatial-restricted labeling, we suggested that a large portion of the adult LCs and other tissue-resident macrophages in the zebrafish were derived from an HSC origin
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data.

claim: The conclusion that adult LCs and tissue-resident macrophages are HSC-derived differs from previous reports in mice suggesting they arise from EMPs born in the YS.
source: This conclusion differed from previous reports in mice suggesting that adult LCs and other tissue-resident macrophages arise from EMPs born in the YS (Ginhoux and Guilliams, 2016; Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015; Hoeffel et al., 2015; Kierdorf et al., 2015; Schulz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous literature supported by citations.

claim: The discrepancy in LC origin conclusions could be due to species differences between zebrafish and mice.
source: One possible explanation for the different conclusions could be the species differences. Zebrafish might differ from mice in terms of the origin of tissue-resident macrophages.
evidence: This is speculation about possible reasons for the discrepancy.

claim: The discrepancy in LC origin conclusions could be due to different fate-mapping methods used.
source: Another explanation was that this discrepancy was due to the different fate-mapping methods used in these studies.
evidence: This is speculation about methodological reasons for the discrepancy.

claim: Sheng et al. showed that most LCs and some other tissue-resident macrophages in adult mice arose from HSCs using the c-Kit-MER-Cre-MER-loxp reporter system.
source: In fact, by utilizing the c-Kit-MER-Cre-MER-loxp reporter system, Sheng et al., showed that most LCs and some other tissue-resident macrophages in adult mice arose from HSCs, which differed from the EMP origin obtained from previous fate-mapping studies using the Runx1-MER-Cre-MER-loxp and Tier2-MER-Cre-MER-loxp reporter systems (Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015; Hoeffel et al., 2015; Schulz et al., 2012; Sheng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sheng et al. study.

claim: A substantial number (30%) of LCs were recorded in 1-year-old Flt3CreRosa26YFP reporter mice.
source: For instance, a substantial number (30%) of LCs were recorded in 1-year-old Flt3CreRosa26YFP reporter mice (Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015), in which HSCs and HSCs-derived hematopoietic progenitors were labeled upon Cre-mediated excision (Christensen and Weissman, 2001; Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gomez Perdiguero et al. study.

claim: In Flt3CreRosa26YFP reporter mice, HSCs and HSC-derived hematopoietic progenitors were labeled upon Cre-mediated excision.
source: For instance, a substantial number (30%) of LCs were recorded in 1-year-old Flt3CreRosa26YFP reporter mice (Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015), in which HSCs and HSCs-derived hematopoietic progenitors were labeled upon Cre-mediated excision (Christensen and Weissman, 2001; Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations about the Flt3Cre system.

claim: It is conceivable that a substantial portion of adult LCs and other tissue-resident macrophages in mice were derived from conventional HSCs born in the AGM.
source: Therefore, it was conceivable that a substantial portion of adult LCs and other tissue-resident macrophages in mice were derived from conventional HSCs born in the AGM.
evidence: This is speculation based on reinterpretation of existing mouse data.

claim: Further in-depth studies in mice with high temporospatially resolved fate mapping are necessary to clarify the origin of LCs.
source: Further in-depth studies in mice with high temporospatially resolved fate mapping will be necessary to clarify this issue.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: The density of HSCs gradually decreased from the anterior to the posterior of the VDA.
source: Our study also reinforced the hypothesis that the density of HSCs gradually decreased from the anterior to the posterior of the VDA.
evidence: This is supported by the position-dependent labeling data in the current study.

claim: The Wnt-Notch signaling pathways and inflammatory signaling cascades are likely to have critical roles in HSC fate determination.
source: We speculated that the Wnt-Notch signaling pathways and inflammatory signaling cascades, which are involved in HSC specification in the VDA (Clements et al., 2011; Espín-Palazón et al., 2014; He et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014), were likely to have critical roles in HSC fate determination.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations about signaling pathways in HSC specification.

claim: The aorta endothelium isolated from different time windows of mouse embryos appears to manifest distinct differentiation potentials, including non-HSC features, under in vitro culture conditions.
source: Several previous studies in mice have shown that the aorta endothelium isolated from different time windows of mouse embryos appears to manifest, at least under in vitro culture conditions, distinct differentiation potentials, including non-HSC features (Bertrand et al., 2005; North et al., 2002; Ody et al., 1999; Taoudi and Medvinsky, 2007; Yoshimoto et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous mouse studies.

claim: A non-HSC population of cells may exist in the mammalian aorta endothelium, similar to zebrafish.
source: These studies suggested that, perhaps similar to zebrafish, this non-HSC population of cells also exists in the mammalian aorta endothelium.
evidence: This is speculation based on inference from mouse studies.
